Because civil forfeiture cases have the absolute minimum standard of evidence. Something called "preponderance of the evidence" which literally means >50% chance that there was a crime, as determined by the judge. It doesn't need to be any specific crime, not one that was worth bringing charges on, just a crime. Doesn't even need to be a crime committed by you, just has to involve the property in some way.

So an officer gets suspicious and this suspicion can be founded on literally anything (remember the department gets the money), and seizes the property as "proceeds of crime." If you want it back you need to spend money on persuading a judge that your property was not proceeds of crime and if, by the end, if the judge still thinks there was a crime somewhere the money is lost, no proof necessary.

It's War on Drugs BS if you couldn't tell, intended as a way to hurt drug dealers when there wasn't enough evidence for conviction (yes, it's a deliberate evasion of due process), and used as a revenue generating tool for police.

It's not a search or seizure under the law, it's a government taking, which technically requires no justification at all. The Fifth Amendment authorizes this at the end:

nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation.

In other words, the state can take anything it wants from you as long as it pays you for it. Americans call this eminent domain and Brits call it compulsory purchase, but it's functionally the same everywhere: the government reserves the right to buy things from you without your permission.
